MUQATIL:24:41-43/r4.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:24:41-43/r4.speaker: author
MUQATIL:24:41-43/r4.claim: God drives and combines clouds, piling their parts upon one another and joining them again, until rain emerges from within.

MUQATIL:24:41-43/r5.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:24:41-43/r5.speaker: author
MUQATIL:24:41-43/r5.claim: The hail comes down from mountains in the sky, striking some people's crops and fruit while being diverted from others.

MUQATIL:24:41-43/r6.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:24:41-43/r6.speaker: author
MUQATIL:24:41-43/r6.claim: The lightning's brightness almost takes away eyesight.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p454/r3.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p454/r3.speaker: author
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p454/r3.claim: God forms clouds, joins them, piles them up, and sends rain from between them; hail descends from mountain-like accumulations in the sky, which are made of hail.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p455/r1.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p455/r1.speaker: author
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p455/r1.claim: Hail can destroy crops, like a cold wind that ruins a people's field; misfortune comes from people's deeds, while God forgives much.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p455/r2.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p455/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p455/r2.claim: When someone said frogs had rained down overnight, Ibn ʿAbbās replied that this was true because the sky contains seas.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p455/r3.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p455/r3.speaker: قتادة
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p455/r3.claim: Qatāda glosses the brightness of the lightning as its light; God can divert hail from whomever He wills.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p455/r4.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p455/r4.speaker: رسول الله
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p455/r4.claim: A report from ʿUrwa b. al-Zubayr says the Prophet instructed people not to point at lightning or rain but to describe it.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p455/r5.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p455/r5.speaker: رسول الله
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p455/r5.claim: A report from Makḥūl says the Prophet urged seeking answered prayer when armies meet, at the establishment of prayer, and when rain descends.

FARRA:v2p256#2/r1.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v2p256#2/r1.speaker: author
FARRA:v2p256#2/r1.claim: الودق means rain, and يصيب به means He punishes with it.

FARRA:v2p256#2/r2.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v2p256#2/r2.speaker: author
FARRA:v2p256#2/r2.claim: The mountains may be actual formations of hail in the sky, with من omitted before the material; alternatively they mean mountain-sized quantities of hail, like two houses' worth of straw.

FARRA:v2p256#2/r3.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v2p256#2/r3.speaker: author
FARRA:v2p256#2/r3.claim: When من introduces material or measure, removing it makes the following noun accusative, as in عدل ذلك صياما and ملء الأرض ذهبا.

FARRA:v2p256#2/r4.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v2p256#2/r4.speaker: أبو جعفر
FARRA:v2p256#2/r4.claim: Abu Ja'far read يذهب بالأبصار in the description of the lightning.

FARRA:v2p256/r1.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v2p256/r1.speaker: author
FARRA:v2p256/r1.claim: بينه can be singular after سحاب because the word is singular in form but collective in meaning; a collective such as نخل likewise permits بين with one noun.

FARRA:v2p256/r2.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v2p256/r2.speaker: author
FARRA:v2p256/r2.claim: بين normally requires two or more referents; a single place-name works only when it denotes a group or a compound settlement, as in the poem about Hूमل and عراد.

MAJAZ:v2p67/r1.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v2p67/r1.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v2p67/r1.claim: Yuzjī means drives or moves along.

MAJAZ:v2p67/r2.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v2p67/r2.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v2p67/r2.claim: Rukāman means piled one mass upon another.

MAJAZ:v2p67/r3.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v2p67/r3.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v2p67/r3.claim: Al-wadq means droplets or rain; ʿĀmir ibn Juwayn's verse uses it for rain falling from a cloud.

MAJAZ:v2p67/r4.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v2p67/r4.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v2p67/r4.claim: Min khilālihi means from between the clouds; khilāl and khalal both mean spaces between, as Zayd al-Khayl's poem shows.

MAJAZ:v2p67/r5.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v2p67/r5.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v2p67/r5.claim: Sanā is shortened and means lightning's brightness, while sanāʾ with a long vowel means honor.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p61#3/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p61#3/r1.speaker: قتادة
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p61#3/r1.claim: Qatada says the lightning's gleam is its flashes, which nearly take away sight.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p306#2/r2.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p306#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p306#2/r2.claim: Rukāman means one mass piled on top of another.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p306#2/r4.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p306#2/r4.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p306#2/r4.claim: Khilālihi means through the gaps between the clouds.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p306#2/r5.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p306#2/r5.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p306#2/r5.claim: Sanā barqihi means the light of its lightning.

TAB-FULL:v17p337/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v17p337/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v17p337/r1.claim: One interpretation takes the phrase literally: God sends hail from mountains in the sky, with the mountains themselves made of hail.

TAB-FULL:v17p337/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v17p337/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v17p337/r2.claim: Another interpretation takes the phrase as an amount of hail as large as mountains falling from the sky, just as “two houses of straw” means an amount of straw filling two houses.

TAB-FULL:v17p339/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v17p339/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v17p339/r1.claim: “Sanā” is the shortened noun for the intense light of the cloud's lightning, nearly blinding whoever sees it.

TAB-FULL:v17p339/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v17p339/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v17p339/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses the lightning's sanā as its light.

TAB-FULL:v17p339/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v17p339/r3.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v17p339/r3.claim: Qatada describes it as the flash of lightning that nearly takes sight away.

TAB-FULL:v17p339/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v17p339/r4.speaker: ابن زيد
TAB-FULL:v17p339/r4.claim: Ibn Zayd says the lightning's brightness can take away sight.

TAB-FULL:v17p339/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v17p339/r5.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v17p339/r5.claim: Most readers pronounce “yadhhab” with an open yāʾ, while Abū Jaʿfar reads it with a ḍamma as a passive verb.

TAB-FULL:v17p339/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v17p339/r6.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v17p339/r6.claim: The open-yāʾ reading is preferred by consensus and Arab usage: “went with it” takes a preposition, while the causative “made it go” normally takes a direct object.

ZAJJAJ:v4p49#2/r1.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v4p49#2/r1.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v4p49#2/r1.claim: The phrase means hail-bearing clouds like mountains, or an amount of hail as great as mountains, as in mountains of wealth.

ZAJJAJ:v4p49#2/r2.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v4p49#2/r2.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v4p49#2/r2.claim: A lightened reading of ينزل is allowed; Abu Jaʿfar alone read يذهب بالأبصار, grammatically weak though the yāʾ form with ḍamma is allowed.

ZAJJAJ:v4p49#2/r3.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v4p49#2/r3.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v4p49#2/r3.claim: Sana is lightning's light; readings distinguish برق as the amount of lightning from برقة as one flash, like an action once versus its measure.

ZAJJAJ:v4p49/r1.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v4p49/r1.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v4p49/r1.claim: Yuzjī means drives, yualif joins scattered clouds into one, and rukāman piles clouds together; wadq is rain.

ZAJJAJ:v4p49/r2.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v4p49/r2.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v4p49/r2.claim: The reading خلاله is broader and better than خلله; khilāl is a plural like mountains from mountain.

ZAJJAJ:v4p49/r3.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v4p49/r3.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v4p49/r3.claim: Cloud may be plural or collective singular; بينه can refer to the whole cloud, as a region name can contain multiple places.

IBNABIHATIM:v8p2617/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2617/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2617/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses the verb “yuzjī” as making ships run.

IBNABIHATIM:v8p2617/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2617/r2.speaker: كعب
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2617/r2.claim: Ka'b says clouds act as a sieve for rain; without them, rain falling directly from the sky would ruin what it struck. He also says the earth's vegetation differs from year to year and seeds descend from heaven.

IBNABIHATIM:v8p2617/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2617/r3.speaker: عطاء
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2617/r3.claim: Clouds emerge from the earth; Ata cites the verse saying God sends winds that stir clouds.

IBNABIHATIM:v8p2617/r4.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2617/r4.speaker: أم عبد الله بنت خالد بن معدان
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2617/r4.claim: A report says a tree in Paradise bears clouds: ripe black cloud-fruit brings rain, while unripe white fruit does not.

IBNABIHATIM:v8p2617/r5.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2617/r5.speaker: عبيد بن عمير
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2617/r5.claim: God sends forces that sweep the earth, create clouds, join them, and pollinate clouds or trees; the transmitter is uncertain whether the final object is cloud or tree.

IBNABIHATIM:v8p2618/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2618/r1.speaker: أبو تميلة عن أبيه
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2618/r1.claim: The word “al-wadq” is interpreted as lightning.

IBNABIHATIM:v8p2618/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2618/r2.speaker: عبد الرحمن بن زيد
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2618/r2.claim: “Through its openings” means through the clouds.

IBNABIHATIM:v8p2618/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2618/r3.speaker: كعب
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2618/r3.claim: Hail descends from the fourth heaven; without it, whatever it passed would be destroyed.

IBNABIHATIM:v8p2618/r4.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2618/r4.speaker: كعب
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2618/r4.claim: Asked about lightning, Ka'b said it is what precedes hail.

IBNABIHATIM:v8p2618/r5.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2618/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2618/r5.claim: “The brightness of its lightning” means the light of its lightning.

IBNABIHATIM:v8p2618/r6.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2618/r6.speaker: عطاء
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2618/r6.claim: The phrase means the light of its lightning almost takes away sight.

IBNABIHATIM:v8p2618/r7.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2618/r7.speaker: قتادة
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2618/r7.claim: The flash of lightning almost takes away sight.

IBNABIHATIM:v8p2619/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2619/r1.speaker: عمرو بن دينار
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2619/r1.claim: He had never seen lightning blind anyone; rather, it sends thunderbolts that strike whomever God wills.

IBNABIHATIM:v8p2619/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2619/r2.speaker: السدي
IBNABIHATIM:v8p2619/r2.claim: The flash of the lightning shines so intensely that it dazzles the eye.

NAHHAS:v3p141/r1.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v3p141/r1.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v3p141/r1.claim: Bayn normally relates two things, but baynahu is possible for clouds as a collective containing many clouds or segments.

NAHHAS:v3p141/r10.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v3p141/r10.speaker: أبو جعفر
NAHHAS:v3p141/r10.claim: He reads yudhhib with a damma on yāʾ; Abu Hatim calls this ungrammatical, following al-Akhfash’s analogy that one says dakhala bi-l-madkhal, not udkhila.

NAHHAS:v3p141/r11.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v3p141/r11.speaker: أبو حاتم
NAHHAS:v3p141/r11.claim: He argues that bāʾ alternates with the hamza of transitivity; the author says that view is clear, though extra bāʾ is also attested elsewhere.

NAHHAS:v3p141/r12.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v3p141/r12.speaker: محمد بن يزيد
NAHHAS:v3p141/r12.claim: He says bāʾ can attach to a verbal noun implied by its verb: ‘its going with the eyes’ or ‘its causing the eyes to go.’

NAHHAS:v3p141/r2.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v3p141/r2.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v3p141/r2.claim: A singular cloud can also take bayn because it includes many parts, like a singular tree containing many branches.

NAHHAS:v3p141/r3.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v3p141/r3.speaker: امرؤ القيس
NAHHAS:v3p141/r3.claim: The verse ‘between al-Dukhūl and Ḥawmal’ uses bayn with one place-name that contains many sites, supporting the collective explanation.

NAHHAS:v3p141/r4.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v3p141/r4.speaker: الأصمعي
NAHHAS:v3p141/r4.claim: He says the construction is not valid and recites ‘between al-Dukhūl and Ḥawmal’ with wāw instead of faʾ.

NAHHAS:v3p141/r5.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v3p141/r5.speaker: ابن عباس والضحاك
NAHHAS:v3p141/r5.claim: They read khalal as the singular of khilāl, whose singular form can denote a plural, like jamal/jimāl.

NAHHAS:v3p141/r6.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v3p141/r6.speaker: الفراء
NAHHAS:v3p141/r6.claim: If the phrase means mountains containing hail, he puts min barad in the genitive and construes the mountains as hail; this requires tanwīn on jibāl.

NAHHAS:v3p141/r7.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v3p141/r7.speaker: البصريون
NAHHAS:v3p141/r7.claim: They allow min barad in the accusative or genitive: the genitive is apposition, while the accusative is a circumstantial accusative for Sibawayh or explanatory for Abu al-Abbas.

NAHHAS:v3p141/r8.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v3p141/r8.speaker: الفراء
NAHHAS:v3p141/r8.claim: If ‘mountains’ means mountain-sized quantities, min barad is accusative only, as in ‘two houses of straw’ and the cited expiation phrase.

NAHHAS:v3p141/r9.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v3p141/r9.speaker: قول مجهول
NAHHAS:v3p141/r9.claim: If min is extra in both phrases, both are accusative only.

FARISI-HUJJA:v5p330#2/r1.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v5p330#2/r1.speaker: ورش عن نافع
FARISI-HUJJA:v5p330#2/r1.claim: Warsh from Nāfiʿ reads يؤلف without pronouncing the hamza, replacing the softened hamza with wāw.

FARISI-HUJJA:v5p330#2/r2.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v5p330#2/r2.speaker: قالون والباقون
FARISI-HUJJA:v5p330#2/r2.claim: Qālūn and the other readers pronounce the hamza; both forms are acceptable because the word derives from joining things and Arabic regularly softens this hamza to wāw.

IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v2p113/r1.author: Ibn Jinnī
IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v2p113/r1.speaker: author
IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v2p113/r1.claim: The variant قيعات may be a plural of قيعة, like ديمة/ديمات, or a plural of قاع, like نار/نيرة; it may also be lengthened قيعة in poetic pronunciation.

IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v2p113/r2.author: Ibn Jinnī
IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v2p113/r2.speaker: author
IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v2p113/r2.claim: If قيعات is a plural, it evokes many separate patches, as in the poem describing foam scattered across lowlands.

IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v2p113/r3.author: Ibn Jinnī
IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v2p113/r3.speaker: طلحة بن مصرف
IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v2p113/r3.claim: Ṭalḥah ibn Muṣarrif reads سَناء برقه with a long alif: سناء means honor, which metaphorically conveys exceptional brightness; the common short form سنا means light.

IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v2p113/r4.author: Ibn Jinnī
IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v2p113/r4.speaker: أبو جعفر يزيد
IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v2p113/r4.claim: Abū Jaʿfar Yazīd reads يُذْهِب with ḍamma on yāʾ, making the lightning remove sight; the bāʾ emphasizes the verb's transitive force.

IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v2p115/r1.author: Ibn Jinnī
IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v2p115/r1.speaker: author
IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v2p115/r1.claim: The bāʾ in يذهب بالأبصار is not empty addition: it reinforces transitivity, or the phrase can mean the lightning almost twists the eyes away or seizes them.

THALABI:v7p112/r10.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v7p112/r10.speaker: author
THALABI:v7p112/r10.claim: سنا برق means the cloud's lightning; its intense brightness nearly takes sight.

THALABI:v7p112/r11.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v7p112/r11.speaker: أبو جعفر
THALABI:v7p112/r11.claim: He reads يذهب with a prefixed damma and a kasra on ha; other readers use the ordinary verb meaning to go away.

THALABI:v7p112/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v7p112/r5.speaker: author
THALABI:v7p112/r5.claim: يزجي means He drives the clouds where He wills and joins their scattered pieces into a mass stacked on itself.

THALABI:v7p112/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v7p112/r6.speaker: author
THALABI:v7p112/r6.claim: The pronoun referring to السحاب is masculine because it follows the word's grammatical form, though السحاب is a collective plural.

THALABI:v7p112/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v7p112/r7.speaker: author
THALABI:v7p112/r7.claim: ودق is rain emerging through the cloud's middle; Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak read من خلله.

THALABI:v7p112/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v7p112/r8.speaker: author
THALABI:v7p112/r8.claim: The phrase about mountains of hail can mean hail itself, or an amount or likeness of mountains; the three من particles mark source, part, and kind.

THALABI:v7p112/r9.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v7p112/r9.speaker: author
THALABI:v7p112/r9.claim: Hail may strike and destroy people, crops, and property, or God may divert it from whomever He wills.

MAWARDI-FULL:v4p112/r1.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p112/r1.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p112/r1.claim: Yuzjī means bringing clouds down gradually; the related phrase describes scant goods.

MAWARDI-FULL:v4p112/r2.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p112/r2.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p112/r2.claim: Alternatively, it means driving clouds wherever one wills.

MAWARDI-FULL:v4p112/r3.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p112/r3.speaker: النابغة
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p112/r3.claim: The poem's verb azjī illustrates driving something.

MAWARDI-FULL:v4p112/r4.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p112/r4.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p112/r4.claim: Clouds are gathered and dispersed as they spread, so they strengthen and join.

MAWARDI-FULL:v4p112/r5.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p112/r5.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p112/r5.claim: Rukāman means piled one upon another.

MAWARDI-FULL:v4p112/r6.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p112/r6.speaker: أبو الأشهب
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p112/r6.claim: Al-wadq may mean lightning emerging through the clouds.

MAWARDI-FULL:v4p112/r7.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p112/r7.speaker: الجمهور
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p112/r7.claim: Most interpreters take al-wadq to mean rain emerging through clouds.

MAWARDI-FULL:v4p112/r8.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p112/r8.speaker: الشاعر
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p112/r8.claim: A poem uses wadq of rain falling from a cloud.

MAWARDI-FULL:v4p113/r1.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p113/r1.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p113/r1.claim: One view posits hail mountains in the sky, from which God sends hail.

MAWARDI-FULL:v4p113/r2.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p113/r2.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p113/r2.claim: Alternatively, hail descends from the sky in mountain-sized masses.

MAWARDI-FULL:v4p113/r3.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p113/r3.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p113/r3.claim: Alternatively, sky means clouds for height and mountains for size; hail or its diversion is punishment or blessing.

MAWARDI-FULL:v4p113/r4.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p113/r4.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p113/r4.claim: Sanā al-barq may mean the sound of lightning.

MAWARDI-FULL:v4p113/r5.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p113/r5.speaker: يحيى بن سلام
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p113/r5.claim: Sanā may mean the lightning's light.

MAWARDI-FULL:v4p113/r6.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p113/r6.speaker: الشماخ
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p113/r6.claim: Al-Shammakh's line uses sanā of lightning's light.

MAWARDI-FULL:v4p113/r7.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p113/r7.speaker: قتادة
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p113/r7.claim: Sanā means gleam; lightning's sound arises from that gleam.

MAWARDI-FULL:v4p113/r8.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p113/r8.speaker: امرؤ القيس
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p113/r8.claim: A poem compares lightning's gleam to lamps.

MAWARDI-FULL:v4p113/r9.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p113/r9.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v4p113/r9.claim: Lightning signals dense clouds and strong rain and warns of thunderbolts.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p319/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p319/r1.speaker: المفسرون وأهل اللغة
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p319/r1.claim: The exegetes and linguists explain يزجي as gently driving or moving clouds along.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p319/r10.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p319/r10.speaker: الزجاج
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p319/r10.claim: Alternatively, al-Zajjaj says سحاب is singular in form but treated as plural because it contains many clouds, as a place-name can contain many locations.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p319/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p319/r2.speaker: المبرد
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p319/r2.claim: Al-Mubarrad says the cloud is moved along swiftly because مزجى means light or easily moved.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p319/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p319/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p319/r3.claim: The author cross-refers the meaning of izjaʾ to the use of مزجاة in 12:88.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p319/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p319/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p319/r4.claim: The underlying form of يؤلف has hamza; Warsh's reading softens it by changing the hamza to waw, and both full articulation and softening are accepted.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p319/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p319/r5.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p319/r5.claim: The softening follows a regular rule for replacing hamza with waw, as in التودة for التؤدة.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p319/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p319/r6.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p319/r6.claim: The basic sense of تأليف is joining one part of a thing to another.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p319/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p319/r7.speaker: أبو إسحاق
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p319/r7.claim: Abu Ishaq says the scattered pieces of cloud are made into one mass.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p319/r8.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p319/r8.speaker: الفراء
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p319/r8.claim: Al-Farra says بين normally requires two or more referents; سحاب is formally singular here but collective in meaning, like نخل or شجر.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p319/r9.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p319/r9.speaker: الزجاج
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p319/r9.claim: Al-Zajjaj allows سحاب to be a collective of clouds, so بينه means between all of them.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p320/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p320/r1.speaker: الليث
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p320/r1.claim: Al-Layth defines ركم as piling one thing over another until it becomes a heap.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p320/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p320/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p320/r2.claim: The author says the cloud is made by stacking some parts of it over others and refers to 8:37 for the same expression.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p320/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p320/r3.speaker: المفسرون
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p320/r3.claim: The exegetes explain الودق as drops or rain.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p320/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p320/r4.speaker: الليث
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p320/r4.claim: Al-Layth says wadq covers rain of every intensity, heavy or light.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p320/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p320/r5.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p320/r5.claim: The word is also used in the expression سحابة وادقة, and a related verb is cited in the source.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p320/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p320/r6.speaker: المبرد
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p320/r6.claim: Al-Mubarrad derives wadq from the rain's emergence from cloud, comparing the usage to something protruding from a body.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p320/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p320/r7.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p320/r7.claim: Cloud apertures are the exits for raindrops; خلال is the plural of خلل, on the pattern جبل/جبال.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p322/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p322/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p322/r1.claim: من خلاله means through the cloud's depths or layers, and the author cross-refers the word to 17:5.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p322/r10.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p322/r10.speaker: الفراء
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p322/r10.claim: Al-Farra's second analysis takes the expression as quantities or sizes of hail comparable to mountains.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p322/r11.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p322/r11.speaker: أبو إسحاق
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p322/r11.claim: Abu Ishaq likewise reads من جبال as an amount as large as mountains, like saying someone has mountains of money.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p322/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p322/r2.speaker: الفراء
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p322/r2.claim: Al-Farra's first analysis takes the mountains as actual formations of hail in the sky, with من explaining their material.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p322/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p322/r3.speaker: أبو إسحاق
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p322/r3.claim: Abu Ishaq reads the phrase as mountains containing hail, like an iron ring held in one's hand.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p322/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p322/r4.speaker: أبو علي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p322/r4.claim: On that syntax, Abu Ali supplies a deleted object: God sends down hail from the mountains, as the parallel ellipsis in 14:48 shows.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p322/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p322/r5.speaker: أبو علي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p322/r5.claim: Abu Ali also permits من to be extra in an affirmative clause, making hail itself the object sent down.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p322/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p322/r6.speaker: المبرد
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p322/r6.claim: Al-Mubarrad chooses the actual mountains made of hail analysis, with the material of the mountains understood and hail as the object of sending.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p322/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p322/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p322/r7.claim: Ibn Abbas says God has told people that there are mountains of hail in the sky.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p322/r8.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p322/r8.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p322/r8.claim: The author says the actual heavenly mountains of hail reading is the established exegetical view and the strongest Arabic analysis.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p322/r9.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p322/r9.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p322/r9.claim: In the preferred analysis, the three من particles respectively mark origin, partitive selection, and the material of which the hail mountains consist.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p325/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p325/r1.speaker: أبو علي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p325/r1.claim: On the figurative reading, mountains signify abundant quantity and grandeur, not actual terrain; Ibn Muqbil's verse uses mountains as an image for poetic abundance.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p325/r10.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p325/r10.speaker: المبرد
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p325/r10.claim: Al-Mubarrad distinguishes short-vowel سنى for flashes from long-vowel سنى for rank and honor, deriving both from brightness.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p325/r11.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p325/r11.speaker: السدي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p325/r11.claim: Al-Suddi says the lightning's radiance nearly flashes away eyesight.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p325/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p325/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p325/r2.claim: The object of sending remains ellipted as in the first syntactic analysis.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p325/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p325/r3.speaker: الليث
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p325/r3.claim: Al-Layth defines hail as frozen rain and uses سحاب برد for a cloud containing hail.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p325/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p325/r4.speaker: مقاتل
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p325/r4.claim: Muqatil says hail harms the crops and fruit of whomever it strikes, while God diverts it from those whose crops He wills to spare.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p325/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p325/r5.speaker: ابن عباس والمفسرون
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p325/r5.claim: Ibn Abbas and the exegetes give a similar explanation of hail striking or sparing crops and fruit.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p325/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p325/r6.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p325/r6.claim: سنا means light or radiance, as in the light of fire, the moon, or lightning.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p325/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p325/r7.speaker: الليث
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p325/r7.claim: Al-Layth uses the verb أسنى for lightning when its radiance enters a house, reaches the ground, or moves in clouds.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p325/r8.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p325/r8.speaker: ابن السكيت
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p325/r8.claim: Ibn al-Sikkit says lightning brightness is written with final alif and has the dual سنوان; al-Asmaʿi knew no verb for it.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p325/r9.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p325/r9.speaker: الكسائي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v16p325/r9.claim: Al-Kisaʾi reports two plural forms for سنا, with the first vowel either damma or kasra.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:24:43-45/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:24:43-45/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:24:43-45/r1.claim: God drives clouds where He wills, joins their pieces and stacks them; rain emerges through their gaps, while hail descends from mountains in the sky, striking some and sparing others, and lightning nearly blinds.

JISHUMI:v7p5217/r2.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v7p5217/r2.speaker: ابن عباس، الضحاك
JISHUMI:v7p5217/r2.claim: The common reading خلاله means the cloud center; Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak give خلله, the plural of خلل.

JISHUMI:v7p5217/r3.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v7p5217/r3.speaker: أبو جعفر
JISHUMI:v7p5217/r3.claim: Abu Jafar reads يذهب with a passive-causative form; the other readers use ذهب يذهب, which the author prefers because the verb is transitive here.

JISHUMI:v7p5218/r1.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v7p5218/r1.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v7p5218/r1.claim: Khalal is the gap between two things; hail is named from cold or from scraping the earth; sana with long vowel means elevation and short sana means sight.

JISHUMI:v7p5218/r4.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v7p5218/r4.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v7p5218/r4.claim: The pronouns in ثم يؤلف بينه ثم يجعله refer to سحاب as a masculine word, and its feminine form is non-literal.

JISHUMI:v7p5218/r5.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v7p5218/r5.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v7p5218/r5.claim: In من السماء من جبال فيها من برد, the first من marks origin, the second a part, and the third explains kind.

JISHUMI:v7p5224/r1.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v7p5224/r1.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v7p5224/r1.claim: Everything indicates God's unity, transcendence, and justice; this is preferable to restricting glorification to some beings or treating it as spoken praise only.

JISHUMI:v7p5224/r3.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v7p5224/r3.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v7p5224/r3.claim: The heavens and earth, birds in flight, clouds, rain and hail, and the alternation of night and day show God's unity and perfect power, knowledge, life, hearing, and sight.

JISHUMI:v7p5224/r4.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v7p5224/r4.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v7p5224/r4.claim: Rainfall follows the choice and purposes of a living, willing God, contrary to natural philosophers.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p53#2/r10.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p53#2/r10.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p53#2/r10.claim: Abū Jaʿfar reads يذهب with initial yāʾ in ḍamma and hāʾ in kasra.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p53#2/r5.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p53#2/r5.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p53#2/r5.claim: God drives and joins clouds, piles them up, and rain emerges through them; wadq is rain and khilāl is their middle.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p53#2/r6.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p53#2/r6.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p53#2/r6.claim: “Mountains of hail” may mean hail descending, with من extra, or an immense quantity like mountains.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p53#2/r7.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p53#2/r7.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p53#2/r7.claim: Another view takes the mountains as actual mountains of hail in the sky; Ibn ʿAbbās says they are there, with hail omitted as the object.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p53#2/r8.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p53#2/r8.speaker: أهل النحو
BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p53#2/r8.claim: The three من particles mark origin, partitive meaning, and kind/material respectively.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p53#2/r9.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p53#2/r9.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p53#2/r9.claim: Hail destroys crops and property, while God diverts it; lightning nearly blinds with its brightness.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p250#2/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p250#2/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p250#2/r1.claim: Yuzji means to drive gently, as in an unwanted, low-grade commodity that everyone passes along.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p250#2/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p250#2/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p250#2/r2.claim: Cloud may be singular or collective; composing one cloud means gathering scattered pieces, so “between it” refers to its parts, as in the poetic place names Dukhul and Hawmal.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p250#2/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p250#2/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p250#2/r3.claim: Rukam is piled cloud, wadq is rain, and khilal are openings; a reading has the singular collective khalal.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p250#2/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p250#2/r4.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p250#2/r4.claim: Readings include intensified yunzilu, assimilated yakadu sana, different forms for lightning flashes and their quantity, and sanaa with short vowel meaning light or long vowel meaning height.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p250#2/r5.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p250#2/r5.speaker: أبو جعفر المدني
KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p250#2/r5.claim: Abu Jaʿfar al-Madani reads “takes away sight” with an extra bā’, as in 2:195.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p250#2/r6.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p250#2/r6.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p250#2/r6.claim: The rain, lightning, and alternation of night and day are clear proofs of God’s lordship and attributes, showing His control of mercy, warning observers to reflect.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p250#2/r7.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p250#2/r7.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p250#2/r7.claim: The Prophet knew the unseen acts described here through God’s revelation, which explains “Have you not seen?”

KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p250#2/r8.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p250#2/r8.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p250#2/r8.claim: The three min phrases may respectively mark origin, partitive division and explanation; alternatively, the first two mark origin and the last is partitive.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p250#2/r9.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p250#2/r9.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p250#2/r9.claim: “Mountains of hail” may mean God creates literal mountains of hail in heaven, or it may express great abundance, as in mountains of gold.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p189/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p189/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p189/r1.claim: The vision is sight by the eye; the implied focus is God's command and power.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p189/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p189/r2.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p189/r2.claim: Yuzji means to drive slowly, used for moving heavy or sluggish things such as clouds and camels.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p189/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p189/r3.speaker: الفرزدق
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p189/r3.claim: Al-Farazdaq's line about slow camels that yuzji-hā illustrates the verb's sense of driving them along.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p189/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p189/r4.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p189/r4.claim: The phrase about merchandise of little value refers to goods requiring intercession and promotion to get them moving, like a heavy load.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p189/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p189/r5.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p189/r5.claim: Yuliffu combines dispersed clouds; the construction between them reflects the gaps inherent in clouds, and between cannot normally take a singular without another item understood.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p189/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p189/r6.speaker: ورش
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p189/r6.claim: Warsh from Nafi does not use hamza in yūlif; Qalun and the other readers pronounce the hamza, which is the basic form.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p189/r7.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p189/r7.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p189/r7.claim: Rukam is piled and compacted cloud; wind compresses it so rain comes out, as in the verse about water pouring from the clouds.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p189/r8.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p189/r8.speaker: حسان بن ثابت
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p189/r8.claim: Hassan's poem about pressed juice compares wine to water pressed from clouds; the Basran judge used it to explain the verse to a litigant.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p189/r9.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p189/r9.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p189/r9.claim: Wadq means rain, as in a poet's description of a cloud releasing its rain and the earth sprouting.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p190/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p190/r1.speaker: الجمهور
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p190/r1.claim: Most read min khilalihi, the plural of khalal; Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak read min khallihi, while Asim and al-Aʿraj intensify yunazzilu.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p190/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p190/r2.speaker: فرقة
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p190/r2.claim: Some take the mountains of hail literally, while others use mountains as a metaphor for abundant hail; al-Akhfash's claim that min before barad is extra is weak.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p190/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p190/r3.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p190/r3.claim: The prepositions distinguish source from heaven, partitive selection from the mountains, and the kind or substance of the hail.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p190/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p190/r4.speaker: الجمهور
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p190/r4.claim: Sana without hamza means light, while sanaʾ with a long vowel means glory or elevation; most read the short form and Talha the long one.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p190/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p190/r5.speaker: طلحة بن مصرف
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p190/r5.claim: Talha reads barqihi as baruqihi, a collective for flashes of lightning, and reads the word with a long hamza as well.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p190/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p190/r6.speaker: أبو جعفر
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p190/r6.claim: Abu Jaʿfar reads yudhhibu with ḍamma, from adh haba; the bāʾ may indicate an appropriate action or resemble a construction with an extra bāʾ.

TABRISI:24:41-45/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:24:41-45/r4.speaker: author
TABRISI:24:41-45/r4.claim: God gently drives clouds, joins their scattered portions, piles them up, and rain emerges through their openings.

TABRISI:24:41-45/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:24:41-45/r5.speaker: author
TABRISI:24:41-45/r5.claim: The mountains of hail may be mountains within the clouds, where hail gathers before falling; al-Balkhī and others hold this view.

TABRISI:24:41-45/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:24:41-45/r6.speaker: الفراء
TABRISI:24:41-45/r6.claim: Al-Farrāʾ interprets the phrase as a quantity of hail as great as mountains, like saying one has two housefuls of straw.

TABRISI:24:41-45/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:24:41-45/r7.speaker: الحسن
TABRISI:24:41-45/r7.claim: Hasan and al-Jubbāʾī take the verse literally as referring to created mountains of hail in the familiar heaven.

TABRISI:24:41-45/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:24:41-45/r8.speaker: author
TABRISI:24:41-45/r8.claim: Hail can destroy crops and property, while God’s withholding it from others is a mercy; sending it is punishment and withholding its harm is blessing.

TABRISI:24:41-45/r9.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:24:41-45/r9.speaker: author
TABRISI:24:41-45/r9.claim: The cloud’s lightning nearly blinds people because of its intense flash, as in the comparison with lightning snatching sight.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p52/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p52/r1.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p52/r1.claim: God drives clouds, joins scattered pieces into one, and piles one layer atop another; although سحاب is grammatically singular, it conveys a collective meaning. الودق means rain of any intensity.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p52/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p52/r2.speaker: ابن مسعود وابن عباس وأبو العالية ومجاهد والضحاك
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p52/r2.claim: They read من خلله rather than من خلاله; the plural of خلل is خلال, as جبال is the plural of جبل.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p52/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p52/r3.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p52/r3.claim: The object of sending down is omitted but understood as hail; من first marks origin, second indicates partitive selection, and third explains the kind of mountains.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p52/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p52/r4.speaker: المفسرون
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p52/r4.claim: They describe mountains in heaven created from hail.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p52/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p52/r5.speaker: الزجاج
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p52/r5.claim: He paraphrases the phrase as hail descending from mountains of hail in heaven, like an iron ring on a hand.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p52/r6.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p52/r6.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p52/r6.claim: The hail may damage crops and fruit; السنا means light.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p52/r7.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p52/r7.speaker: مجاهد وأبو جعفر
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p52/r7.claim: They read يذهب with ḍamma on yāʾ and kasra on hāʾ.

RAZI-FULL:v24p12#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v24p12#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v24p12#2/r1.claim: “Do you not see” calls for sight by the mind; izjāʾ means to drive gently and gradually, as in a small consignment and in moving camels at an easy pace.

RAZI-FULL:v24p12#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v24p12#2/r2.speaker: الفراء
RAZI-FULL:v24p12#2/r2.claim: Al-Farra says bayna normally takes two or more nouns; the singular pronoun here is explained because cloud is formally singular but collective in meaning.

RAZI-FULL:v24p12#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v24p12#2/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v24p12#2/r3.claim: Joining means bringing cloud fragments together into one cloud.

RAZI-FULL:v24p12#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v24p12#2/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v24p12#2/r4.claim: Rukām means gathered or piled, stacking one thing above another until it forms a heap.

RAZI-FULL:v24p12#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v24p12#2/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
RAZI-FULL:v24p12#2/r5.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses wadq as rain.

RAZI-FULL:v24p12#2/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v24p12#2/r7.speaker: أبو مسلم الأصفهاني
RAZI-FULL:v24p12#2/r7.claim: Abu Muslim al-Isfahani glosses wadq as water.

RAZI-FULL:v24p12#2/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v24p12#2/r8.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v24p12#2/r8.claim: Khilāl means the cloud's gaps and openings; it is the plural of khalal, like mountains is the plural of mountain.

RAZI-FULL:v24p12#2/r9.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v24p12#2/r9.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v24p12#2/r9.claim: A variant reading is reported for the word min at the start of the phrase “from mountains.”

RAZI-FULL:v24p13#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v24p13#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v24p13#2/r1.claim: Every body's particular rising, falling, fineness, density, heat, and cold requires a determiner; if God creates natures and their effects, He is the creator of clouds and rain as well.

RAZI-FULL:v24p13#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v24p13#2/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v24p13#2/r2.claim: God creates the natures that move vapor from the earth into the air; when rising vapors accumulate and adhere, He makes them piled clouds, demonstrating His power and wisdom.

RAZI-FULL:v24p13/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v24p13/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v24p13/r1.claim: Cloud formation may mean that God creates clouds successively, or that He transforms other bodies into cloud; on the latter view He creates the qualities that make them clouds.

RAZI-FULL:v24p13/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v24p13/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v24p13/r2.claim: “Then He joins it” implies that cloud parts already existed separately, since joining requires existing things; stacking lets clouds hold much water.

RAZI-FULL:v24p13/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v24p13/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v24p13/r3.claim: Cloud formation, rain, snow, hail, dew, and frost are wonders of God's creation and signs of His dominion and power.

RAZI-FULL:v24p13/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v24p13/r4.speaker: أهل الطبائع
RAZI-FULL:v24p13/r4.claim: Natural philosophers say clouds and precipitation usually arise by vapor condensation and less often by air condensation; heat can dissolve small quantities of rising vapor.

RAZI-FULL:v24p13/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v24p13/r5.speaker: أهل الطبائع
RAZI-FULL:v24p13/r5.claim: When plentiful vapor reaches a cold layer, moderate cold condenses it into cloud and rain; strong cold freezes it into snow before droplets coalesce or hail afterward.

RAZI-FULL:v24p13/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v24p13/r6.speaker: أهل الطبائع
RAZI-FULL:v24p13/r6.claim: Vapor that remains below the cold layer may gather into rain clouds; five causes of that gathering include blocked ascent, pressure by winds or mountains, colliding winds, a slowed heavy leading part, and strong low-level cold.

RAZI-FULL:v24p13/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v24p13/r7.speaker: أهل الطبائع
RAZI-FULL:v24p13/r7.claim: Low, fine vapor cooled at night condenses into scattered moisture; if it does not freeze it is dew, and if it freezes it is frost, as snow relates to rain.

RAZI-FULL:v24p13/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v24p13/r8.speaker: أهل الطبائع
RAZI-FULL:v24p13/r8.claim: They also explain clouds through contraction of air as it cools.

RAZI-FULL:v24p13/r9.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v24p13/r9.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v24p13/r9.claim: Al-Razi says one cannot assert the natural philosophers' account as necessary, since God may create cloud particles all at once; even if their process occurs, possible bodies still require an efficient cause.

RAZI-FULL:v24p14#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v24p14#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v24p14#2/r1.claim: Readings include assimilated “sanā barqihi,” a plural barqah for a flash or measure of lightning, and “sanāʾ” with a long vowel; the short form means light and the long form height.

RAZI-FULL:v24p14#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v24p14#2/r2.speaker: أبو جعفر المدني
RAZI-FULL:v24p14#2/r2.claim: Abu Jaʿfar al-Madani reads the bāʾ as extra in “yadhhab bil-abṣār,” with a parallel construction in the prohibition against casting oneself into destruction.

RAZI-FULL:v24p14#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v24p14#2/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v24p14#2/r3.claim: Lightning nearly taking sight must be powerful, pure fire; its appearance from hail, its opposite, demonstrates the work of a wise and capable agent.

RAZI-FULL:v24p14#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v24p14#2/r4.speaker: النحويون
RAZI-FULL:v24p14#2/r4.claim: Grammarians dispute whether saying “I took Zayd to the house” requires the speaker to go there too; those denying that requirement cite this verse.

RAZI-FULL:v24p14#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v24p14#2/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v24p14#2/r5.claim: God's turning of night and day can mean their alternation, one entering into the other, or changes such as cold and heat; all meanings can apply because they bring benefit and reflection.

RAZI-FULL:v24p14#2/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v24p14#2/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v24p14#2/r6.claim: The preceding phenomena provide evidence to people of insight and show that people should reflect on them, undermining blind imitation.

RAZI-FULL:v24p14/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v24p14/r1.speaker: مجاهد
RAZI-FULL:v24p14/r1.claim: The majority of commentators, including Mujahid and al-Kalbi, understand the phrase literally: God created mountains of hail in the sky and sends down from them what He wills.

RAZI-FULL:v24p14/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v24p14/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v24p14/r2.claim: A second view calls elevated cloud the sky and compares massive clouds to mountains; hail is frozen water created in cloud, and the cloud may be called mountains because it is made of hail.

RAZI-FULL:v24p14/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v24p14/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v24p14/r3.claim: Al-Razi prefers literal mountains of hail: “sky” properly names the particular celestial body, while taking it as cloud is figurative; since either is within God's power, the apparent reading should stand.

RAZI-FULL:v24p14/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v24p14/r4.speaker: أبو علي الفارسي
RAZI-FULL:v24p14/r4.claim: Abu Ali al-Farisi parses the three min particles respectively as marking origin, partitive selection, and explanation of the hail's substance; the object of “sends down” is omitted but understood.

RAZI-FULL:v24p14/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v24p14/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v24p14/r5.claim: The pronoun in “strikes by it” refers to hail: it can harm animals and plants, but God sends it where wise and diverts its harm by preventing it from falling elsewhere.

RAZI-FULL:v24p14/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v24p14/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v24p14/r6.claim: Reading hail as stones and their descent as a punishment of annihilation is a remote interpretation.

QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44#2/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44#2/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44#2/r1.claim: Rukām means piled together in layers, as in the piled cloud of another verse; the root means collecting one thing upon another.

QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44#2/r10.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44#2/r10.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44#2/r10.claim: The hail strikes whom God wills as a punishment and is turned away from whom He wills as a blessing; a report says a particular glorification on hearing thunder protects from harm.

QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44#2/r11.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44#2/r11.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44#2/r11.claim: The lightning’s brilliance almost takes sight; sanna is the brightness of the cloud’s lightning.

QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44#2/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44#2/r2.speaker: أبو الأشهب العقيلي
QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44#2/r2.claim: Abu al-Ashhab al-Uqayli interprets wadq as lightning, supported by a poetic comparison of dust emerging like wadq from cloud openings.

QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44#2/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44#2/r3.speaker: الجمهور
QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44#2/r3.claim: Most commentators say wadq is rain, and lines by an unnamed poet and Imru al-Qays use it for falling drops and rain.

QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44#2/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44#2/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44#2/r4.claim: Khilāl is the plural of khalal, the gaps and channels from which rain comes; the word also means being among a group.

QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44#2/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44#2/r5.speaker: كعب
QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44#2/r5.claim: Kaʿb says clouds are a sieve for rain; without them, water falling from the sky would ruin what it struck on earth.

QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44#2/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44#2/r6.speaker: ابن عباس والضحاك وأبو العالية
QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44#2/r6.claim: Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak, and Abu al-Aliya read khilal in the singular form khalal.

QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44#2/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44#2/r7.speaker: الفراء
QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44#2/r7.claim: One explanation has mountains of hail in the sky, from which hail descends, with the omitted object supplied; al-Farra can treat the mountains themselves as hail.

QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44#2/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44#2/r8.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44#2/r8.claim: Other readings say God created mountains in the sky that contain hail, or that hail descends in an amount or likeness of mountains; the repeated min can mark origin, partitive sense, and material.

QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44#2/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44#2/r9.speaker: الأخفش
QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44#2/r9.claim: Al-Akhfash treats both min before mountains and min before hail as extra, parsing mountains and hail as objects: hail descends like mountains.

QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44#3/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44#3/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44#3/r1.claim: Sana in the short form means lightning’s flash and is also the name of a medicinal plant; the long form sanāʾ means elevation, though both share the sense of shining.

QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44#3/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44#3/r2.speaker: طلحة بن مصرف
QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44#3/r2.claim: Talha reads the long form sanāʾ for intense brightness and purity; al-Mubarrad distinguishes short-form flash from long-form rank and honor.

QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44#3/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44#3/r3.speaker: طلحة بن مصرف
QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44#3/r3.claim: Talha’s other reading, sanāʾ barqihi, is said by Ahmad ibn Yahya to use a plural of barqa, a flash or measure of lightning.

QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44#3/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44#3/r4.speaker: الجحدري وابن القعقاع
QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44#3/r4.claim: They read yudhhibu in form IV, with bāʾ extra; the rest read yadhhabu, with bāʾ indicating attachment to the eyes.

QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44#3/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44#3/r5.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44#3/r5.claim: Lightning signals dense clouds and likely heavy rain while warning of possible lightning strikes.

QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44/r1.claim: The verse presents another proof of God’s power and asks whether one sees with the eye of the heart.

QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44/r2.claim: Yuzjī means to drive or guide along; Arabic uses it for wind driving clouds, a cow driving her calf, and easily collected tax.

QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44/r3.speaker: النابغة
QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44/r3.claim: Al-Nabigha’s lines use azjī and tuzjī for leading along a remnant of life and driving snow clouds with the north wind.

QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44/r4.claim: The clouds are joined as they form so they grow connected and dense; the basic verb is hamzated, though a lightened waw reading is reported.

QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44/r5.speaker: الفراء والزجاج والأصمعي
QURTUBI-FULL:24:43-44/r5.claim: Though cloud is singular in form, baynahu can refer to its collective meaning or to its many parts; al-Asmaʿi rejects this and prefers the reading that names the two places.

BAYDAWI-FULL:24:42-43/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:24:42-43/r2.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:24:42-43/r2.claim: God gently drives and joins scattered clouds, piles them up, and sends rain through their openings; Warsh reads يولف without hamza.

BAYDAWI-FULL:24:42-43/r3.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:24:42-43/r3.speaker: نافع برواية ورش
BAYDAWI-FULL:24:42-43/r3.claim: Warsh's transmission from Nafi reads يولف without a hamza.

BAYDAWI-FULL:24:42-43/r4.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:24:42-43/r4.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:24:42-43/r4.claim: Hail mountains can mean huge or solid pieces from the sky; the syntax permits من to mark the hail's material or amount, with an implied object for sends.

BAYDAWI-FULL:24:42-43/r5.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:24:42-43/r5.speaker: قيل
BAYDAWI-FULL:24:42-43/r5.claim: Another view takes the sky as the visible canopy containing literal hail mountains, like stone mountains on earth; reason alone does not rule it out.

BAYDAWI-FULL:24:42-43/r6.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:24:42-43/r6.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:24:42-43/r6.claim: The familiar account says vapor rises, forms cloud in cold air, and becomes rain, snow, or hail depending on cold and condensation; all requires the will of the Wise Necessary Being.

BAYDAWI-FULL:24:42-43/r7.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:24:42-43/r7.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:24:42-43/r7.claim: The hail's lightning nearly blinds observers with its intense light, a strong proof of God's power in bringing opposites together.

BAYDAWI-FULL:24:42-43/r8.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:24:42-43/r8.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:24:42-43/r8.claim: The brightness phrase has readings with a long vowel, assimilation, variant vowels in barq, or an added preposition.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p150#4/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p150#4/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p150#4/r1.claim: God drives clouds where He wills; saḥāb is a plural of saḥābah, and the masculine pronoun follows the word's grammatical gender.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p150#4/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p150#4/r2.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p150#4/r2.claim: Clouds are joined together and piled into a mass; wādq is rain emerging through their gaps.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p150#4/r3.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p150#4/r3.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p150#4/r3.claim: “From the sky” may mark the starting point; “from mountains” can indicate a portion, with hail descending from heavenly mountains.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p150#4/r4.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p150#4/r4.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p150#4/r4.claim: Another parsing treats “from” in the two first occurrences as a starting point and the last as partitive; alternatively, God creates mountains of hail in the sky or the phrase magnifies quantity like mountains of gold.

NASAFI-FULL:v3p150#4/r5.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v3p150#4/r5.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v3p150#4/r5.claim: The hail strikes people and crops, or it punishes whomever God wills and is withheld from others; the lightning's glow nearly steals sight.

QASHANI:24:43-44#2/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:24:43-44#2/r1.speaker: author
QASHANI:24:43-44#2/r1.claim: Lightning is a flash of knowledge that vanishes until it becomes established; its brilliance overwhelms inner sight with bewilderment, which means increased knowledge and light.

QASHANI:24:43-44#2/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:24:43-44#2/r2.speaker: author
QASHANI:24:43-44#2/r2.claim: The Prophet’s prayer to increase bewilderment is interpreted as a request for increased knowledge and light.

QASHANI:24:43-44/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:24:43-44/r1.speaker: author
QASHANI:24:43-44/r1.claim: Clouds signify branches of intellect drawn from particular images by inspirations and volitions, then combined into syllogistic arrangements that yield conclusions.

QASHANI:24:43-44/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:24:43-44/r2.speaker: author
QASHANI:24:43-44/r2.claim: Rain signifies resulting certain knowledge; mountains in the spirit’s sky are lights of tranquility, certainty, and repose.

QASHANI:24:43-44/r3.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:24:43-44/r3.speaker: author
QASHANI:24:43-44/r3.claim: Hail may represent revealed realities and intuitive meanings, or the spirit’s mountains may be innate repositories of sciences, explaining why different people acquire disciplines with different ease.

QASHANI:24:43-44/r4.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:24:43-44/r4.speaker: author
QASHANI:24:43-44/r4.claim: The descending knowledge reaches spiritual faculties God wills and is turned away from veiled psychic faculties.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p56/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p56/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p56/r5.claim: Cloud and rain imagery follows the return to God as evidence of His control in changing states and anticipating resurrection; yuzjī means to drive gently and gradually, as with a heavy cloud or camel.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p56/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p56/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p56/r6.claim: Cloud is a collective noun; God moves one cloud toward another, joins their parts, and piles them densely so rain emerges through gaps formed by their compression.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p56/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p56/r7.speaker: ورش
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p56/r7.claim: Warsh reads “yuʾallif” with wāw; the other seven readers use hamza.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p56/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p56/r8.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p56/r8.claim: “Khilāl” is explained either as a singular or as a plural of khalal; Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and others read the singular “khalal.”

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p56/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p56/r9.speaker: مجاهد
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p56/r9.claim: The apparent meaning, held by Mujāhid, al-Kalbī, and most commentators, is that there are mountains of hail in the sky like mountains of stone on earth; others take “mountains” as a metaphor for abundance or an ellipsis of comparison.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p57/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p57/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p57/r1.claim: Al-Ḥūfī's appositional parse of the second “min” as referring to the sky fails: if it replaces the first, both must mark origin, as in “from Baghdad, from al-Karkh.”

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p57/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p57/r2.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p57/r2.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya take the second “min” as partitive and the last as explanatory, so hail is the thing sent down from some sky-mountains.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p57/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p57/r3.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p57/r3.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī also allows the first two “min” particles to indicate origin and the final one to be partitive, making hail descend from mountains in the sky.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p57/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p57/r4.speaker: الأخفش
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p57/r4.claim: Al-Akhfash treats the second and third “min” particles as redundant, with “mountains containing hail” as the direct object; al-Farrāʾ similarly says hail gathers like mountains for dramatic effect.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p57/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p57/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p57/r5.claim: Another parse makes the first two “min” particles indicate origin and the third redundant, yielding hail from the mountains of the sky.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p57/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p57/r6.speaker: الزجاج
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p57/r6.claim: Al-Zajjāj compares the construction to an iron ring in one's hand: “of hail” qualifies the mountains and the object sent down is from those mountains, which must therefore be made of hail.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p58/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p58/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p58/r1.claim: The pronoun in “with it” apparently refers to hail, but may refer to rain and hail together; rain more commonly brings harm, while diverting hail is a greater benefit and favor.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p58/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p58/r2.speaker: طلحة بن مصرف
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p58/r2.claim: The usual reading is short “sanā” with singular “barq”; Ṭalḥa reads long “sanāʾ” and plural “buruq,” with another form harmonizing the two vowel marks. “Sanāʾ” means elevation or rank.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p58/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p58/r3.speaker: أبو جعفر
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p58/r3.claim: Abū Jaʿfar reads “yudhhib” passively; al-Akhfash and Abū Ḥātim criticize it, but the author defends it as transmitted and notes that Shayba also reads it so.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p58/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p58/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p58/r4.claim: The passive reading is parsed either with an added bāʾ or with bāʾ meaning “from” and an omitted object, “removes the light from eyes”; a verse supports the latter usage.

SAMIN-DURR:24:43#2/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:24:43#2/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:24:43#2/r1.claim: فيها alone may describe the mountains, with من برد as its subject because the phrase is governed.

SAMIN-DURR:24:43#2/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:24:43#2/r2.speaker: الزجاج
SAMIN-DURR:24:43#2/r2.claim: Al-Zajjaj paraphrases the verse as hail-bearing mountains from the sky; min separates phrase elements while preserving the sense of an iron ring in a hand, making من برد an adjective of جبال.

SAMIN-DURR:24:43#2/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:24:43#2/r3.speaker: أبو البقاء
SAMIN-DURR:24:43#2/r3.claim: Abu al-Baqa prefers an omitted شيء, yielding some of the mountains, since فيها من برد would otherwise need an antecedent object.

SAMIN-DURR:24:43#2/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:24:43#2/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:24:43#2/r4.claim: The author objects that the pronoun in فيها can refer to السماء, so Abu al-Baqa's extra omitted noun is unnecessary and his conclusion contradicts his own claim.

SAMIN-DURR:24:43#2/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:24:43#2/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:24:43#2/r5.claim: The pronoun in به may refer to hail alone or to both rain and hail, using the pronoun like a demonstrative.

SAMIN-DURR:24:43#3/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:24:43#3/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:24:43#3/r1.claim: Short سنا means light and derives from a wāw root; Imru al-Qays uses سناه for brightness.

SAMIN-DURR:24:43#3/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:24:43#3/r2.speaker: شاعر مجهول
SAMIN-DURR:24:43#3/r2.claim: A cited poem uses سناء for elevation or eminence, the long-vowel homonym.

SAMIN-DURR:24:43#3/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:24:43#3/r3.speaker: ابن وثاب
SAMIN-DURR:24:43#3/r3.claim: Ibn Waththab reads سناء with lengthening, analogizing tangible lightning in the sky to a person's intangible height.

SAMIN-DURR:24:43#3/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:24:43#3/r4.speaker: ابن وثاب
SAMIN-DURR:24:43#3/r4.claim: He reads برقه as برقة with ḍamma on bāʾ, a plural meaning a portion of lightning; a second transmission has ḍamma on rāʾ by vowel assimilation.

SAMIN-DURR:24:43#3/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:24:43#3/r5.speaker: العامة
SAMIN-DURR:24:43#3/r5.claim: The common reading has يذهب with fatḥa on yāʾ and hāʾ.

SAMIN-DURR:24:43#3/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:24:43#3/r6.speaker: أبو جعفر
SAMIN-DURR:24:43#3/r6.claim: Abu Jafar reads يُذهب with ḍamma on yāʾ and kasra on hāʾ, from the causative form.

SAMIN-DURR:24:43#3/r7.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:24:43#3/r7.speaker: الأخفش وأبو حاتم
SAMIN-DURR:24:43#3/r7.claim: Al-Akhfash and Abu Hatim reject this reading on the grounds that ب substitutes for hamza.

SAMIN-DURR:24:43#3/r8.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:24:43#3/r8.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:24:43#3/r8.claim: The author defends Abu Jafar's reading: ب may be extra, as in 23:20, or the object may be omitted and ب mean من, so the light departs from eyes; poetry supports the latter.

SAMIN-DURR:24:43/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:24:43/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:24:43/r1.claim: بينه can take the singular pronoun because السحاب is generic; alternatively an إضافة is omitted, meaning between its cloud-pieces, each piece being a cloud.

SAMIN-DURR:24:43/r10.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:24:43/r10.speaker: الحوفي والزمخشري
SAMIN-DURR:24:43/r10.claim: For the third من, they add a fourth possibility, بيان الجنس: the mountains themselves are hail, so the descending object is mountains of hail.

SAMIN-DURR:24:43/r11.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:24:43/r11.speaker: الزمخشري
SAMIN-DURR:24:43/r11.claim: Al-Zamakhshari also combines origin for the first two منs with partitive sense for the third, making the direct object some hail from the sky's mountains.

SAMIN-DURR:24:43/r12.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:24:43/r12.speaker: الأخفش والفراء
SAMIN-DURR:24:43/r12.claim: If the second and third من are extra, al-Akhfash makes the phrase an بدل of the first, while al-Farra makes the second object of ينزل and the third a predicate, with the resulting clause adjectival to جبال.

SAMIN-DURR:24:43/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:24:43/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:24:43/r2.claim: خلال may be singular like حجاب or plural like جبال; Ibn Masud and al-Dahhak's singular خلله, also reported from Abu Amr, supports the singular analysis.

SAMIN-DURR:24:43/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:24:43/r3.speaker: قيل
SAMIN-DURR:24:43/r3.claim: الودق is explained as rain, whether light or heavy; a poetic line uses it for rain from a cloud.

SAMIN-DURR:24:43/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:24:43/r4.speaker: قيل
SAMIN-DURR:24:43/r4.claim: Another gloss takes الودق as lightning, supported by a poem comparing its appearance through cloud to الودق through cloud gaps.

SAMIN-DURR:24:43/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:24:43/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:24:43/r5.claim: الودق is originally a verbal noun, and يخرج is circumstantial because the verb تَرَى is visual.

SAMIN-DURR:24:43/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:24:43/r6.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:24:43/r6.claim: The first من marks origin without disagreement.

SAMIN-DURR:24:43/r7.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:24:43/r7.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:24:43/r7.claim: The second من may also mark origin, with its phrase as an بدل of the first; it may mark partitive meaning for al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya, or be extra, yielding mountains descending.

SAMIN-DURR:24:43/r8.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:24:43/r8.speaker: الزمخشري وابن عطية
SAMIN-DURR:24:43/r8.claim: They take the second من as partitive, making the mountains' portion the object of ينزل; al-Hawfi calls من جبال a بدل while also treating it as partitive.

SAMIN-DURR:24:43/r9.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:24:43/r9.speaker: الشيخ
SAMIN-DURR:24:43/r9.claim: The Shaykh rejects al-Hawfi's mixed بدل analysis: true بدل requires the two prepositions to share a meaning, as in travel from Baghdad from al-Karkh.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p72#2/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p72#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p72#2/r1.claim: God first gently drives newly formed clouds, gathers their scattered parts, piles them atop one another, and sends rain through them.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p72#2/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p72#2/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p72#2/r2.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḍaḥḥāk read the phrase as rain emerging through the cloud's openings.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p72#2/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p72#2/r3.speaker: عبيد بن عمير الليثي
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p72#2/r3.claim: ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr describes winds that sweep the earth, raise clouds, assemble them, and fertilize them with rain-bearing water; Ibn Abī Ḥātim and al-Ṭabarī transmit this account.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p72#2/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p72#2/r4.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p72#2/r4.claim: Grammarians parse the three min particles as origin, partitive, and explanatory if hail comes from mountain-like formations in the sky; on the cloud interpretation, the second min is also origin and apposition to the first.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p73/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p73/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p73/r1.claim: The hail and rain may strike as mercy and be withheld as delayed rain; alternatively, hail may punish by scattering fruit and destroying crops and trees, while its being withheld is mercy.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p73/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p73/r2.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p73/r2.claim: The lightning's intense light nearly snatches sight when someone follows or looks directly at it.

BIQAI-FULL:v5p272/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v5p272/r2.speaker: أبو حيان
BIQAI-FULL:v5p272/r2.claim: Abu Hayyan says izjāʾ is used for gently driving a heavy thing; sḥāb is a generic noun whose singular is saḥāba, and the phrase means driving one cloud toward another.

BIQAI-FULL:v5p272/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v5p272/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v5p272/r3.claim: God creates clouds from nothing, sometimes low and sometimes high, initially thin and scattered, then joins their parts and piles them into a massive mass.

BIQAI-FULL:v5p272/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v5p272/r4.speaker: القزاز
BIQAI-FULL:v5p272/r4.claim: Al-Qazzaz explains al-wadq as rain, while another view takes it as the abundance of rain.

BIQAI-FULL:v5p272/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v5p272/r5.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v5p272/r5.claim: Rain emerges through openings formed in the piled cloud as its parts press and condense against one another.

BIQAI-FULL:v5p272/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v5p272/r6.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v5p272/r6.claim: The mountains in the sky are clouds amassed until they resemble mountains; hail is frozen water, and God sends or withholds rain and hail by choice as mercy or punishment.

BIQAI-FULL:v5p272/r7.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v5p272/r7.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v5p272/r7.claim: Lightning nearly blinds with its brilliant flashes; its strength signals dense clouds and heavy rain and warns of possible lightning strikes.

BIQAI-FULL:v5p272/r8.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v5p272/r8.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v5p272/r8.claim: God alternates night and day, light and darkness, increase and decrease, rain and clear skies, producing heat, cold, growth, and dryness; these changes show power, comprehensive knowledge, and oneness to reflective observers.

DURR-FULL:v6p211/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v6p211/r1.speaker: الضحاك
DURR-FULL:v6p211/r1.claim: Al-Dahhak glosses al-wadaq as rain; Mujahid glosses it as drops of rain, while Abu Bujayla’s father says it is lightning.

DURR-FULL:v6p211/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v6p211/r2.speaker: ابن زيد
DURR-FULL:v6p211/r2.claim: Ibn Zayd says ‘through it’ means through the cloud; Ibn Abbas read the phrase with an open khāʾ and no alif.

DURR-FULL:v6p211/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v6p211/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v6p211/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas reads lightning’s sana as its light; Nafiʿ ibn al-Azraq asks about this meaning, which Ibn Abbas supports with a line by Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith witnessing the word sanāh.

DURR-FULL:v6p211/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v6p211/r4.speaker: قتادة
DURR-FULL:v6p211/r4.claim: Qatada glosses the lightning’s sana as its flashing brightness.

DURR-FULL:v6p211/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v6p211/r5.speaker: كعب
DURR-FULL:v6p211/r5.claim: Kaʿb says hail falling from the fourth heaven would destroy anything it passed; he also told ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr that lightning is what precedes hail.

BURSEVI:v6p119#2/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p119#2/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v6p119#2/r3.claim: يزجي means gently and easily driving something along, especially an insignificant thing; this hints that clouds are negligible relative to God's power. Clouds are named for their movement through air, and here the plural parts are intended.

BURSEVI:v6p119#2/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p119#2/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v6p119#2/r4.claim: The verse describes seeing God visually guide clouds wherever He wills.

BURSEVI:v6p119#3/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p119#3/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v6p119#3/r1.claim: God joins separate cloud portions into one, then piles them on top of one another; ركام means a gathered mass.

BURSEVI:v6p119#3/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p119#3/r2.speaker: أبو الليث
BURSEVI:v6p119#3/r2.claim: Abu al-Layth defines الودق as all rain, whether heavy or light.

BURSEVI:v6p119#3/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p119#3/r3.speaker: المفردات
BURSEVI:v6p119#3/r3.claim: Al-Mufradat reports an alternative definition of الودق as the dust-like material visible among raindrops, also used for rain itself.

BURSEVI:v6p119#3/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p119#3/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v6p119#3/r4.claim: The gap phrase is circumstantial with visual seeing; cloud openings are the spaces between things and here are passages through which drops emerge.

BURSEVI:v6p119#3/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p119#3/r5.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v6p119#3/r5.claim: The rain comes out from the cloud's gaps and openings created by the accumulation and compression of its parts.

BURSEVI:v6p119#3/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p119#3/r6.speaker: كعب
BURSEVI:v6p119#3/r6.claim: Ka'b says clouds act as a sieve for rain; without them rain would ruin what it struck.

BURSEVI:v6p119#3/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p119#3/r7.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v6p119#3/r7.claim: Here السماء means the clouds, since anything above you is called sky, and the sky is the highest part of anything.

BURSEVI:v6p119#4/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p119#4/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v6p119#4/r1.claim: The hail comes from immense chunks resembling mountains, located in the sky; sky is grammatically feminine here.

BURSEVI:v6p119#4/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p119#4/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v6p119#4/r2.claim: The preposition من before hail marks the object as partitive, while the earlier instances mark source and the second is an appositive relation; hail is frozen water.

BURSEVI:v6p119#4/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p119#4/r3.speaker: بعضهم
BURSEVI:v6p119#4/r3.claim: One view says God made mountains of ice and snow in the sky and assigned an angel to release measured hail or snow onto a region by His command.

BURSEVI:v6p119#4/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p119#4/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
BURSEVI:v6p119#4/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas says every spring running on earth ultimately comes from snow and ice.

BURSEVI:v6p119#4/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p119#4/r5.speaker: قيل
BURSEVI:v6p119#4/r5.claim: Another report says angels are half ice and half fire; by flapping their wings they send down the snow that falls from them.

BURSEVI:v6p119#4/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p119#4/r6.speaker: قيل
BURSEVI:v6p119#4/r6.claim: An alternative takes the sky as the encompassing celestial sphere containing mountains of hail, like the stone mountains on earth; reason does not rule it out.

BURSEVI:v6p119#4/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p119#4/r7.speaker: المشهور
BURSEVI:v6p119#4/r7.claim: The familiar natural account says rising vapor forms cloud in cold air: moderate cold yields rain, stronger cold yields hail before vapor joins, and extreme cold can condense air into cloud and rain or snow; all remains governed by divine will and wisdom.

BURSEVI:v6p119#4/r8.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p119#4/r8.speaker: إخوان الصفاء
BURSEVI:v6p119#4/r8.claim: Ikhwan al-Safa explain that fine cloud differs from dense cloud; rain falls when water particles join, cool, and grow heavy, hail freezes after leaving cloud, and snow freezes within it.

BURSEVI:v6p120/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p120/r1.speaker: ابن التمجيد
BURSEVI:v6p120/r1.claim: Ibn al-Tamjid says sunlight on dry ground breaks off fiery particles that combine with earthy particles to form smoke.

BURSEVI:v6p120/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p120/r2.speaker: شرح القانون
BURSEVI:v6p120/r2.claim: Sharh al-Qanun distinguishes smoke, made from earth and fire, from vapor, made from water and air; vapor is finer.

BURSEVI:v6p120/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p120/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v6p120/r3.claim: God directs hail toward whom He wills, potentially harming people, crops, livestock, and fruit, and protects others from its danger.

BURSEVI:v6p120/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p120/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v6p120/r4.claim: سنا with a short final vowel means bright light, while the extended form means height; lightning is the cloud's flash.
