BURSEVI:v6p120/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p120/r5.speaker: القاموس
BURSEVI:v6p120/r5.claim: Al-Qamus defines lightning either as a flash of cloud or as an angel striking and moving the cloud so that fires appear.

BURSEVI:v6p120/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p120/r6.speaker: إخوان الصفاء
BURSEVI:v6p120/r6.claim: Ikhwan al-Safa describe lightning as fire sparked by friction among smoky particles inside the cloud.

BURSEVI:v6p120/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v6p120/r7.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v6p120/r7.claim: The lightning nearly takes sight because of its extreme brightness and speed.

ALUSI-FULL:v18p189#3/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v18p189#3/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v18p189#3/r1.claim: The cloud sign confirms what precedes; izjāʾ means moving gently and easily; association with insignificant items suggests clouds are negligible before God’s power.

ALUSI-FULL:v18p189#3/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v18p189#3/r10.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v18p189#3/r10.claim: ‘Mountains’ may mean huge cloud masses; the claim that they are things God created from hail is linguistically unsupported.

ALUSI-FULL:v18p189#3/r11.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v18p189#3/r11.speaker: الأصبهاني
ALUSI-FULL:v18p189#3/r11.claim: Al-Aṣbahānī says mountains are things God created from hail, a reading rejected as unsupported by language.

ALUSI-FULL:v18p189#3/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v18p189#3/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v18p189#3/r2.claim: God may join one cloud to another; alternatively al-saḥāb is one mass whose parts are joined, supplying the plurality bayna requires.

ALUSI-FULL:v18p189#3/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v18p189#3/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v18p189#3/r3.claim: The phrase ‘between the entrance and Ḥawmal’ illustrates bayna with implied plurality; treating clouds as a collective noun is another solution.

ALUSI-FULL:v18p189#3/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v18p189#3/r4.speaker: ورش عن نافع
ALUSI-FULL:v18p189#3/r4.claim: Warsh from Nāfiʿ reads yuʾallifu without hamza.

ALUSI-FULL:v18p189#3/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v18p189#3/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v18p189#3/r5.claim: Rukām means clouds piling atop one another; wadq means rain emerging after accumulation.

ALUSI-FULL:v18p189#3/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v18p189#3/r6.speaker: أبو بحيلة عن أبيه
ALUSI-FULL:v18p189#3/r6.claim: Abū Buḥayla’s father reportedly glosses wadq as lightning, but al-Ālūsī has not seen this elsewhere; most exegesis and lexicons define it as rain.

ALUSI-FULL:v18p189#3/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v18p189#3/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v18p189#3/r7.claim: Kh ilāl are openings formed by accumulation and compression, plural of khall; alternatively singular for a kind, supported by readings from Ibn ʿAbbās and others.

ALUSI-FULL:v18p189#3/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v18p189#3/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v18p189#3/r8.claim: Rain’s emergence is a circumstantial clause; describing it as seen emerging intensifies speed, like the sea splitting after Moses strikes it.

ALUSI-FULL:v18p189#3/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v18p189#3/r9.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v18p189#3/r9.claim: ‘From the sky’ may mean clouds, since anything above is sky, or the upper direction; naming the sky suggests height’s role in precipitation.

ALUSI-FULL:v18p190/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v18p190/r1.speaker: الحوفي
ALUSI-FULL:v18p190/r1.claim: Al-Ḥawfī takes the second min as partitive like the third and also as apposition; al-Ālūsī calls this a clear error.

ALUSI-FULL:v18p190/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v18p190/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v18p190/r2.claim: One parse makes the first min origin, second partitive in object position, and third explanatory: some mountains or hail mountains in the sky descend, namely hail.

ALUSI-FULL:v18p190/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v18p190/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v18p190/r3.claim: Hail strikes whom God wills, harming property and person, while He diverts it from others; the pronouns most naturally refer to hail.

ALUSI-FULL:v18p190/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v18p190/r4.speaker: الأخفش
ALUSI-FULL:v18p190/r4.claim: Al-Akhfash treats the second and third min as additional, with the first phrase object and second appositional, yielding hail from the sky.

ALUSI-FULL:v18p190/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v18p190/r5.speaker: الفراء
ALUSI-FULL:v18p190/r5.claim: Al-Farrāʾ considers both particles additional; the first phrase is object, while the second may say hail rather than stones is in the mountains, with its pronoun referring to mountains.

ALUSI-FULL:v18p190/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v18p190/r6.speaker: ابن مقبل
ALUSI-FULL:v18p190/r6.claim: Ibn Muqbil’s poetry about mountains of poetry illustrates mountain as metaphor for abundance; expressions also speak of mountains of gold or knowledge.

ALUSI-FULL:v18p190/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v18p190/r7.speaker: مجاهد والكلبي وأكثر المفسرين
ALUSI-FULL:v18p190/r7.claim: Mujāhid, al-Kalbī, and most exegetes take sky and mountains literally: God created mountains of hail in the sky as stone mountains on earth, and reason has no decisive objection.

ALUSI-FULL:v18p190/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v18p190/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v18p190/r8.claim: A natural-philosophical account traces rain, snow, hail, and frost to celestial forces, vapor, cooling, and condensation, with wind and heat shaping the outcomes.

ALUSI-FULL:v18p190/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v18p190/r9.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v18p190/r9.claim: All such processes depend on God’s will and wisdom; natural causes are customary and celestial first causes make ‘from the sky’ apt. This account preserves eloquence and avoids popular doubts.

ALUSI-FULL:v18p191/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v18p191/r1.speaker: البحر
ALUSI-FULL:v18p191/r1.claim: Al-Baḥr suggests the pronouns could refer to rain, which more commonly benefits and is directed or withheld; al-Ālūsī considers this remote and objectionable.

ALUSI-FULL:v18p191/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v18p191/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v18p191/r2.claim: Lightning belongs to the cloud above; its possessive precedes explicit mention because existence is obvious, and referring it to hail is rejected.

ALUSI-FULL:v18p191/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v18p191/r3.speaker: طلحة بن مصرف
ALUSI-FULL:v18p191/r3.claim: Ṭalḥa reads sanāʾ long and barq with bāʾ and rāʾ open as plural barqah; another variant follows the bāʾ’s vowel, while sanāʾ denotes elevation and intense light.

ALUSI-FULL:v18p191/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v18p191/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v18p191/r4.claim: Another reading assimilates dāl into sīn in yakādu sanā; lightning nearly overwhelms sight by sudden intensity, and ‘eyes’ heightens the threat.

ALUSI-FULL:v18p191/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v18p191/r5.speaker: أبو جعفر
ALUSI-FULL:v18p191/r5.claim: Abū Jaʿfar reads yudhhibu with ḍamma on yāʾ and kasra on hāʾ; critics fault its transitivity markers, but al-Ālūsī defends the transmitted reading.

ALUSI-FULL:v18p191/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v18p191/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v18p191/r6.claim: The reading may add bāʾ, making ‘eyes’ the object, or use bāʾ meaning ‘from’ with ‘light’ understood; al-Ḥarīrī allows both transitivity markers.

ALUSI-FULL:v18p191/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v18p191/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v18p191/r7.claim: Lightning producing the opposite of its dark cloud is a strong sign of God’s complete power.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p260#2/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p260#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p260#2/r1.claim: Weather signs follow the account of inspired guidance in animals: even inanimate matter follows its fixed divine course better than unbelievers with minds and senses, showing power, knowledge, and oneness.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p260#2/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p260#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p260#2/r2.claim: The sequence of weather events is evidence for God’s power, wisdom, and knowledge, transitioning naturally to that argument.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p260#2/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p260#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p260#2/r3.claim: Yuzjī means drives; God’s measured bringing of clouds together is likened to driving them until they become dense.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p260#2/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p260#2/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p260#2/r4.claim: Joining the clouds is described as bringing their parts together; the cloud discussion is linked to 2:164 and 13:12.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p260#2/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p260#2/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p260#2/r5.claim: Bayna takes a pronoun for cloud because clouds contain parts, as in Imruʾ al-Qays’s phrase between al-Dukhūl and Ḥawmal.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p260#2/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p260#2/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p260#2/r6.claim: Rukām derives from piling and means piled up; the pattern conveys a passive sense, as in 52:44.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p260#2/r7.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p260#2/r7.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p260#2/r7.claim: Some commentators identify the electrical discharge formed by stacked clouds as wadq; most say wadq is rain, the lexical-dictionary meaning, which exits through cloud gaps.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p261/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p261/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p261/r1.claim: Khilāl means openings or gaps, plural of khalal; 17:5 uses the same word.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p261/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p261/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p261/r2.claim: Min al-samāʾ means falling from higher to lower, from the atmosphere to earth; here samāʾ means the sky above a given area of land.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p261/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p261/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p261/r3.claim: Min jibāl is a partitive apposition to al-samāʾ, with the mountains meaning cloud formations like mountains.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p261/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p261/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p261/r4.claim: Calling something a mountain conveys great quantity; the Bukhārī report about a mountain of gold means the speaker would not want it to remain three nights, except money set aside for a debt.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p261/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p261/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p261/r5.claim: The min before jibāl and the first min are origin; the min in min barad is either extra in an affirmative sentence according to some grammarians or a noun meaning some.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p261/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p261/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p261/r6.claim: The object of yunzilu is omitted but supplied by the phrase about hail inside the clouds: He sends down hail.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p261/r7.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p261/r7.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p261/r7.claim: Using min before barad also matches the preceding min jibāl.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p262/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p262/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p262/r1.claim: Calling hail’s descent an ‘impact’ conveys harm, as muṣība means a painful occurrence; 9:50 shows ʾaṣāba can also indicate an ordinary event when context says good fortune.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p262/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p262/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p262/r2.claim: The root of aṣāba is ṣawb, descent, as in rain; hail is an impact because it damages crops, and the pronoun refers to hail.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p262/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p262/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p262/r3.claim: The lightning description modifies the cloud and prompts reflection: people overlook familiar cloud formation, rain, and hail but remember lightning’s striking flashes as a sign of power.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p262/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p262/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p262/r4.claim: Sana, without final hamza, means light of lightning or fire; sanāʾ with hamza means eminence, as shown by Ibn Durayd’s verse.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p262/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p262/r5.speaker: ابن دريد
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p262/r5.claim: Ibn Durayd’s verse distinguishes the shortened and lengthened forms of sanā by contrasting light with honor.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p262/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p262/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p262/r6.claim: The definite article in al-abṣār denotes the class of eyes; the near-blinding lightning recalls 2:20, but this verse adds sanā because it focuses on cloud and rain as signs.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p262/r7.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p262/r7.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p262/r7.claim: In 2:20 the lightning belongs to a threatening portrait of hypocrites: rain seems beneficial but hides thunder, lightning, and calamities.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p263/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p263/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p263/r1.claim: The wording in 24:43 says lightning almost removes eyesight, while 2:20 says it snatches eyesight; snatching conveys attack and domination beyond mere removal.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p263/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p263/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p263/r2.claim: The definite al-abṣār means the class of eyesight, as in 12:13 and the phrase enter the market; 2:20 instead specifies their eyes to rebuke them.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p263/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p263/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p263/r3.claim: The two versions vary a shared idea without needless repetition, preserving equal length and displaying the Qurʾān’s eloquence.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p263/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p263/r4.speaker: الجمهور
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p263/r4.claim: The majority read yadhhab with open yāʾ and hāʾ; the bāʾ is causative, meaning it takes away eyesight.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p263/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p263/r5.speaker: أبو جعفر
IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p263/r5.claim: Abū Jaʿfar alone reads yudhhib with a rounded yāʾ and kasra on hāʾ; the bāʾ is extra to emphasize attachment, as in 5:6.

TABATABAI:24:43/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:24:43/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:24:43/r1.claim: Izjāʾ means to drive, rukām means piled up, wadq is rain, and khilāl are gaps; the address to the Prophet as hearer extends to every observer.

TABATABAI:24:43/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:24:43/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:24:43/r2.claim: God drives separate clouds by winds, joins and piles them up, and rain emerges through their gaps.

TABATABAI:24:43/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:24:43/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:24:43/r3.claim: The upper sky is the direction above; mountains of hail describes its abundance and accumulation, and sanāʾ means light.

TABATABAI:24:43/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:24:43/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:24:43/r4.claim: God sends accumulated hail that can ruin fields and gardens and sometimes kill people or livestock, while sparing whom He wills; lightning nearly blinds the eyes.

TABATABAI:24:43/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:24:43/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:24:43/r5.claim: The weather signs explain why God's special light belongs to whom He wills: He may send beneficial rain or damaging hail, choosing who is struck and spared.

TABATABAI:24:43/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:24:43/r6.speaker: author
TABATABAI:24:43/r6.claim: The following alternation of night and day further demonstrates that events are governed solely by God's will.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p288/r5.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p288/r5.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p288/r5.claim: Signs in the world show that God alone controls the universe and that all creation glorifies Him; humans therefore owe Him faith and exclusive worship.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:24:43/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:24:43/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:24:43/r1.claim: The account of rain, lightning, and hail accords with known natural processes but attributes them to God’s permission, will, power, wisdom, and customary law, urging people to observe and learn.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:24:43/r2.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:24:43/r2.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:24:43/r2.claim: The Arabic word wadq can mean rain, but the author translates it as lightning because lightning comes from gaps in clouds; rain falls when clouds turn to rain.

QIRAAT-ER:24:43:20#1/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:24:43:20#1/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:24:43:20#1/r1.claim: Form IV suggests a single descent rather than Form II's staged or repeated descent.

QIRAAT-ER:24:43:41#1/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:24:43:41#1/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:24:43:41#1/r1.claim: Form IV makes the verb causative, shifting from light going away by itself to being directly removed.

STUDYQURAN:24:43/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:24:43/r1.speaker: Some
STUDYQURAN:24:43/r1.claim: Some read the phrase about mountains of clouds as describing how the clouds appear.

STUDYQURAN:24:43/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:24:43/r2.speaker: Others
STUDYQURAN:24:43/r2.claim: Others parse the phrase grammatically as saying that a mountain's worth of hail descends.

STUDYQURAN:24:43/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:24:43/r3.speaker: Th
STUDYQURAN:24:43/r3.claim: Hail is interpreted as an instrument of destruction, as with the destructive clouds in 46:24.

STUDYQURAN:24:43/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:24:43/r4.speaker: Aj
STUDYQURAN:24:43/r4.claim: Clouds usually bring beneficial rain, which symbolizes spiritual blessings reaching the believer's heart.

STUDYQURAN:24:43/r5.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:24:43/r5.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:24:43/r5.claim: The image of lightning nearly blinding people also appears in 2:20.

STUDYQURAN:24:intro/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:24:intro/r3.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:24:intro/r3.claim: The title comes from the Light Verse; the surah's mirage, sea-darkness, and lightning parables use light to depict human inner reality.
